summary: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory alkaloid indicated for prophylaxis and treatment of gout flares in adults and for familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) in adults and children 4 years and older. It binds tubulin, inhibits microtubule polymerization and neutrophil activation/migration, and interferes with inflammasome-mediated IL-1beta activation. For a gout flare the dose is 1.2 mg at the first sign followed by 0.6 mg one hour later; prophylaxis is 0.6 mg once or twice daily (max 1.2 mg/day). Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index and is FATAL IN OVERDOSE. It is a substrate of P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4: in patients with renal or hepatic impairment it must NOT be combined with P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and dose reduction is required in these patients - life-threatening and fatal toxicity has occurred at therapeutic doses in this setting.
indications: Prophylaxis of gout flares in adults
Treatment of acute gout flares in adults (taken at the first sign of a flare)
Treatment of familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) in adults and children 4 years of age and older

moa: Colchicine disrupts cytoskeletal function by inhibiting beta-tubulin polymerization into microtubules, thereby preventing the activation, degranulation and migration of neutrophils that mediate gout inflammation. In FMF, evidence suggests it interferes with intracellular assembly of the inflammasome complex in neutrophils and monocytes that drives activation of interleukin-1beta.

absolute: Patients with both renal OR hepatic impairment AND concomitant P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (includes all protease inhibitors except fosamprenavir) - fatal toxicity reported
monitor: Signs of GI or neuromuscular toxicity

preg: Available published data over several decades have not identified clear drug-associated risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal/fetal outcomes. Colchicine crosses the human placenta. It may be used in pregnancy when clearly needed (particularly to control FMF), weighing benefit and risk.
lact: Colchicine is present in human milk; limited data have not shown adverse effects in breastfed infants at maternal therapeutic doses. May be used during lactation with monitoring of the infant; consider timing of doses.
renal: Reduce the dose or lengthen the interval in renal impairment. Colchicine is not removed by hemodialysis. In renal impairment, do NOT coadminister with P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - fatal toxicity has occurred.
hepatic: Reduce the dose in hepatic impairment. In hepatic impairment, do NOT coadminister with P-gp or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - life-threatening and fatal toxicity has been reported at therapeutic doses.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir and other protease inhibitors) - markedly increase colchicine levels; can be fatal, especially with renal/hepatic impairment
P-glycoprotein inhibitors (cyclosporine, ranolazine) - increase colchicine exposure; dose reduction required, contraindicated in renal/hepatic impairment
moderate: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (diltiazem, verapamil, fluconazole, grapefruit juice) - raise colchicine levels; reduce dose
minor: Other agents causing myelosuppression - additive risk
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to meals; avoid grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition).
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it may worsen GI side effects and provoke gout.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause myelosuppression (low WBC/platelets), raised CK, and abnormal liver enzymes; reversible azoospermia reported.

serious: Bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia)
emergency: Signs of colchicine overdose (severe GI symptoms, dehydration, then multiorgan failure)
Severe cytopenia with infection or bleeding

monitoring: Review of interacting drugs at each visit
Signs and symptoms of GI or neuromuscular toxicity
counsel: For a gout attack take 1.2 mg at the first twinge, then 0.6 mg one hour later - do not keep taking it to treat ongoing pain
Tell your doctor about all medicines - some antibiotics, antifungals and heart drugs can make colchicine dangerously toxic
Stop and seek help if you develop severe diarrhea/vomiting, muscle pain or weakness, numbness, unusual bleeding or signs of infection
This drug can be fatal in overdose - keep it well out of reach of children
Your dose may be lower if you have kidney or liver problems
pk: GI/anti-inflammatory effect within hours; flare relief over the first day
Mean Cmax about 2.5 ng/mL at 1-2 hours (single fasting dose)
Elimination half-life approximately 27-31 hours (multiple dosing); substrate of P-gp and CYP3A4
Prolonged tissue retention; not removed by hemodialysis
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: FATAL IN OVERDOSE - narrow therapeutic index; ingestion above 0.8 mg/kg has been associated with 100% mortality
Dose-reduce and AVOID combining with strong CYP3A4 + P-gp inhibitors in patients with renal or hepatic impairment - fatal interactions at therapeutic doses
Gout flare regimen is 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later - higher/extended dosing adds toxicity without benefit
Not removed by hemodialysis - prevention of toxicity is essential
Watch for myelosuppression and rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins/fibrates
missed: For gout prophylaxis or FMF, take a missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; do not double up. For acute flare treatment the dosing is a one-time course at flare onset, not a regular schedule.
overdose: Colchicine overdose is life-threatening and may be fatal. The exact toxic dose is unknown - deaths have occurred after as little as 7 mg; ingestion above 0.8 mg/kg has shown 100% mortality. Stage 1 (within 24 h): severe GI symptoms with fluid loss and volume depletion, peripheral leukocytosis. Stage 2 (24-72 h): multiorgan failure, with death from respiratory depression and cardiovascular collapse. Survivors may have rebound leukocytosis and alopecia about a week later. There is no specific antidote (colchicine-specific Fab is not generally available); treatment is aggressive supportive care - it is NOT removed by hemodialysis.
